transcript.text: LG F4V5VYP0W says OE and the clothes are sat in water. I'm not opening the little door at the bottom because last time I did that it flooded the whole kitchen. What else can I do?

OE means the washer has been unable to drain within its allowed time, which is why it has left the clothes in water. You do not need to open the bottom filter first: with it switched off and unplugged, pull it forward only if safe and check the drain hose at the back is not kinked, crushed or trapped, and that its end has not been pushed too far down or sealed tightly into the waste pipe. If the hose is clear, a blocked pump filter or something caught in the pump is more likely. In that case the water will need draining, but it can be done slowly with towels and a very shallow tray rather than letting the whole drum empty at once; if you do not want to tackle that, an appliance engineer can drain and clear it without flooding the kitchen.
Ok, the machine is pushed right back against the wall and the hose was squashed behind it, so I've pulled it out and straightened it. What now?

The squashed hose is a very plausible cause of the OE fault, so the next step is simply to test it before opening the filter. Put the machine back safely, ensure the drain hose is not trapped again, then select Drain/Spin and let it try to empty; do not move or open anything while it is running. If it now drains, cancel the programme once empty and run a short rinse to confirm the fault has cleared. If it hums but no water leaves, the remaining likely cause is a blockage at the pump filter/pump; if it is completely silent, the drain pump or its wiring becomes more likely.
I tried the drain/spin again. It drained a little slower than normal and then OE came up again. Still water in the drum. I'm still not unscrewing that filter.

Before you start, switch it off and unplug it. Straightening the crushed hose has helped a little, but the OE return with water still in the drum means there is still a drainage restriction. The most likely cause is a partial blockage in the pump filter or pump, with a blocked household waste connection or a weak drain pump also possible. As you do not want to open the filter, do not force it: an engineer can drain the machine safely and clear the filter/pump without flooding the kitchen. One useful clue before arranging that is whether it hummed or buzzed from the lower front while attempting to drain: humming points more to a blockage; silence makes the pump or its electrical supply more likely.
Yes it hums when it tries to drain, and sometimes there's an occasional rattle too. My husband could do the filter at the weekend, so would that be better than an engineer?

Yes — having your husband check and clear the drain filter first is the better next step than booking an engineer straight away. The humming and occasional rattle, with only slow partial draining, most strongly suggest something caught in the filter or just behind it; the earlier crushed hose may have contributed but does not appear to be the whole fault. With the machine switched off and unplugged, keep the door shut, put towels down and use a very shallow tray. If there is a small emergency drain hose behind the flap, drain it a little at a time into the tray; otherwise loosen the filter only a fraction at a time, emptying the tray between releases. Once the water is down, remove the filter, clear any debris, and use a torch to check the small impeller in the opening: it should move gently and not be jammed, though it may have a slightly stepped feel. Refit the filter fully and straight, then try Drain/Spin. If it still hums and will not empty despite a clear filter and freely moving impeller, or the impeller is loose/broken, the drain pump or a deeper hose blockage needs an engineer.

candidates: Blocked drain-pump filter or pump blockage (high)
Kinked or blocked external drain hose/standpipe (medium)
